Bow and Arrow
BOH and AIR-oh
n. phrase
Bow: Hebrew qesheth, Greek toxon; arrow: Hebrew chēts, Greek belos. The principal long-range weapon of ancient warfare; biblically significant from the Genesis rainbow (my bow in the cloud, Gen 9:13) through Jonathan’s arrows-of-friendship to David, to the apocalyptic horseman of Revelation with the bow.

📖 Biblical Definition

The bow-and-arrow is the principal long-range weapon of ancient warfare and appears across the biblical canon in several substantive theological contexts. First, the rainbow as the LORD’s bow in the cloud. Genesis 9:13 records the post-flood covenant sign: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth. The Hebrew word is qesheth—the same word used elsewhere for the warrior’s bow. The imagery is theologically striking: the LORD has set His warrior’s bow in the cloud, pointed upward toward heaven and away from the earth, as the visible covenantal sign that He will not again destroy the earth by flood. The warrior-bow, hung up and pointed away, becomes the peace-symbol of the post-flood covenant. Second, the bow as the warrior’s instrument. Genesis 27:3 (Isaac to Esau): now therefore take, I pray thee, thy weapons, thy quiver and thy bow, and go out to the field, and take me some venison. Genesis 48:22 (Jacob’s blessing on Joseph): moreover I have given to thee one portion above thy brethren, which I took out of the hand of the Amorite with my sword and with my bow. Genesis 49:24 (Jacob’s blessing on Joseph again): but his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob. The bow is repeatedly associated with the warrior’s strength, the patriarch’s might, and (in Joseph’s blessing) the LORD’s strengthening of the bow that abides in strength. Third, the Jonathan-David narrative. 1 Samuel 18-20 records the deep friendship between Jonathan and David; the climax of their parting is the arrow-signal at 1 Sam 20:35-42, where Jonathan’s arrows shot beyond the lad signal to David that he must flee for his life. The arrows-of-friendship become the means by which Jonathan saves David’s life from Saul’s pursuit. David’s lament for Jonathan in 2 Sam 1:17-27 includes the famous title the song of the bow, taught to the children of Judah as a memorial of Jonathan’s death and David’s grief. Fourth, the apocalyptic horseman of Rev 6:2: and I saw, and behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him: and he went forth conquering, and to conquer. The first horseman of the apocalypse carries a bow, with disputed identification (some read this as Christ Himself going forth to conquer through the gospel; others read it as a figure of warfare and conquest as eschatological judgment). Fifth, the figurative-spiritual uses. The wicked are said to bend their bows against the righteous (Ps 11:2; 64:3-4); the saints’ children are like arrows in the hand of a mighty man (Ps 127:4-5); the LORD’s bow is bent against the wicked (Ps 7:12-13); the apostles are sent forth as bows in the LORD’s hand. The bow-and-arrow doctrine therefore covers a remarkable range: the LORD’s covenant-bow in the cloud, the warrior’s instrument of strength, the arrows of life-saving friendship, the apocalyptic horseman, and the various figurative-spiritual uses across the Psalms.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Compound entry.) The bow-and-arrow is the principal long-range weapon of ancient warfare; biblically significant in the Genesis rainbow as the LORD’s covenant-bow in the cloud (Gen 9:13), the warrior’s instrument of strength, Jonathan’s arrows-of-friendship to David, the apocalyptic horseman of Revelation, and the various figurative-spiritual uses across the Psalms.

BOW, n. — A weapon made of a strip of wood or other elastic material, used for shooting arrows; the principal long-range weapon of ancient warfare.

ARROW, n. — A missile weapon of offense, slender, pointed, and made to be shot with a bow; in scripture, used both literally and figuratively (the saints’ children as arrows in Ps 127:4-5; the wicked’s tongue as a sharp arrow in Ps 64:3).

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 9:13 — "I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth."

Genesis 49:24 — "But his bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob; (from thence is the shepherd, the stone of Israel:)."

1 Samuel 20:36 — "And he said unto his lad, Run, find out now the arrows which I shoot. And as the lad ran, he shot an arrow beyond him."

Psalm 127:4-5 — "As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them: they shall not be ashamed, but they shall speak with the enemies in the gate."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The bow-and-arrow doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the general loss of attention to biblical-warfare imagery in much contemporary preaching, which misses the substantive theological substance the various bow-references carry—the covenant-bow in the cloud as post-flood peace-symbol, the warrior-bow as imagery of God-given strength, the arrows-of-friendship in the Jonathan-David narrative, and the apocalyptic-horseman imagery of Revelation 6.

expand to see more

The general loss of attention to biblical-warfare imagery in much contemporary preaching has dropped substantive doctrinal content the bow-and-arrow references carry. The Genesis 9 rainbow-as-bow is one example: the modern reader sees the rainbow as a pretty post-storm sky-phenomenon without recognizing the theologically loaded imagery of the LORD’s warrior-bow hung up in the cloud and pointed away from the earth. The Hebrew qesheth is the warrior’s weapon, and the rainbow’s bow-shape in the cloud is the visible covenantal sign that the LORD has hung up His bow—the post-flood covenant of peace is symbolized by the war-bow now displayed as no-longer-used-against-the-earth. The recovery of attention to this imagery transforms the rainbow from a generic divine-promise-symbol into the specific war-bow-hung-up post-flood peace-pledge it actually is. The other bow-references carry similar substantive content the loss of warfare-imagery-attention has obscured.

The deeper substance is the comprehensive biblical theology of warfare-imagery that the bow-and-arrow references participate in. Scripture is unembarrassed about military imagery; the LORD is named a man of war (Ex 15:3); His armies are arrayed; His weapons are deployed; the spiritual warfare of the New Testament continues the theme with the believer’s armor-of-God. The bow-and-arrow takes its place in this comprehensive warfare-theology: the covenant-bow as peace-pledge after judgment, the warrior-bow as God-given strength, the arrows-of-friendship in providential-deliverance narratives, the apocalyptic-bow of eschatological judgment. The contemporary believer who has been trained out of warfare-imagery (often by the contemporary cultural distaste for military metaphors in religion) has lost an entire register of biblical doctrine. The recovery is the recovery of the biblical comfort with warfare-imagery in its proper biblical place: the LORD as warrior, the saint as soldier, the bow-and-arrow as one of several weapons in the divine arsenal that biblical doctrine variously deploys.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qesheth (bow) and chēts (arrow); Greek toxon (bow) and belos (arrow, fiery dart); the principal long-range weapon of ancient warfare; biblically significant in the Genesis 9 covenant-bow in the cloud, the patriarchal warrior-bow, the Jonathan-David arrows-of-friendship, the apocalyptic horseman of Rev 6:2, and the various figurative-spiritual uses across the Psalms.

expand to see more

Hebrew qesheth (H7198) — bow (over 75 OT uses; also the rainbow of Gen 9:13).

Hebrew chēts (H2671) — arrow (over 50 OT uses).

Greek toxon (G5115) — bow (Rev 6:2, the only NT use).

Greek belos (G956) — arrow, dart (Eph 6:16, the fiery darts of the wicked quenched by the shield of faith).

Usage

"I do set my bow in the cloud—Gen 9:13’s rainbow as the LORD’s warrior-bow hung up after the flood, post-judgment covenant of peace."

"His bow abode in strength, and the arms of his hands were made strong by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob—Gen 49:24’s imagery of God-given warrior strength."

"Loss of biblical warfare-imagery drops substantive content the bow-and-arrow references carry; recovery is the comfort with warfare-imagery in its proper biblical place: LORD as warrior, saint as soldier, bow-and-arrow as one of several weapons in the divine arsenal."
